connection: Session 31 created TimeClockDbContext, entity mapping, and an EF-backed repository with integration-test infrastructure. Add provider-executed EF Core queries and verify them against SQLite.
objectives: Read ClockEntryDataQueries.CompletedForEmployee's real IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity> return type, and contrast it with GetEmployeeClockEntries's IEnumerable<ClockEntry> from Session 23.
Explain what 'the provider translates the query' means concretely: db.ClockEntries.Where(...) becomes a SQL WHERE clause, not an in-process filter loop.
Trace MaterializeAsync's real await query.ToListAsync(cancellationToken) as the point where the translated SQL actually executes against SQLite.
Predict what would happen if CompletedForEmployee's Where clause referenced a C# method with no SQL equivalent, and why that would fail only when the query is materialized, not when it is built.

visuals.title: IQueryable<T> builds an expression tree, not a filter loop
visuals.explanation: db.ClockEntries.Where(entry => entry.EmployeeId == employeeId && entry.ClockOut != null) records what to filter, without running the filter in C# at all.

visuals.title: The provider translates the expression into SQL
visuals.explanation: EF Core's SQLite provider turns that same expression tree into a real SQL WHERE clause, sent to the database rather than evaluated by the .NET runtime.

visuals.title: ToListAsync is where execution actually happens
visuals.explanation: MaterializeAsync's await query.ToListAsync(cancellationToken) is the moment the translated SQL runs against the database and results come back as ClockEntryEntity objects.

visuals.title: IEnumerable<T> (Session 23) never leaves the process; IQueryable<T> does
visuals.explanation: GetEmployeeClockEntries's Where runs entirely in .NET's memory; CompletedForEmployee's Where is executed by SQLite, outside the .NET process boundary entirely.

preQuiz.prompt: What is different about where db.ClockEntries.Where(...) actually executes, compared to Session 23's _clockEntries.Where(...)?
options: db.ClockEntries.Where's expression tree is translated by EF Core's provider into SQL and executed inside the SQLite database itself; _clockEntries.Where runs entirely inside the .NET process, filtering objects already in memory
They execute identically -- IQueryable and IEnumerable behave the same way
db.ClockEntries.Where executes immediately, before MaterializeAsync is called
preQuiz.explanation: This is the real, concrete difference Session 23 promised to revisit: IQueryable<T>'s deferred execution defers all the way to a database provider, not just to enumeration.

preQuiz.prompt: When does CompletedForEmployee's Where clause actually run against the SQLite database?
options: Only when MaterializeAsync calls query.ToListAsync(...) -- CompletedForEmployee itself only builds the query, without executing it
Every time the ClockEntryEntity objects are read afterward
preQuiz.explanation: ToListAsync is the real materialization point -- exactly the same deferred-until-enumerated principle from Session 23, applied here to database execution instead of in-process enumeration.

preQuiz.prompt: If CompletedForEmployee's Where clause called a C# method SQLite's provider cannot translate to SQL, when would that failure surface?
options: At ToListAsync -- when the provider actually attempts translation -- not when CompletedForEmployee itself builds the expression tree, since building it does not require the provider to understand it yet
preQuiz.explanation: This is a real, subtle consequence of deferred, provider-translated execution: a query can be built successfully and only fail once the provider tries to turn it into SQL.

concept.title: IQueryable<T>: an expression tree, waiting for a provider
paragraphs: ClockEntryDataQueries.CompletedForEmployee returns IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity> -- db.ClockEntries.Where(...) builds a description of the filter as an expression tree, not a filtered list.

Nothing has executed yet at the point CompletedForEmployee returns -- this mirrors Session 23's IEnumerable<ClockEntry> deferred execution, but the eventual translator is a database provider instead of the .NET runtime itself.

concept.title: ToListAsync: where the SQL actually runs
paragraphs: MaterializeAsync's await query.ToListAsync(cancellationToken) is the real execution point -- EF Core's SQLite provider translates the expression tree into an actual SQL statement here, sends it to the database, and maps the returned rows back into ClockEntryEntity objects.

The real, existing test proves this end to end: it opens a genuine (in-memory) SQLite connection, adds a completed entity, and confirms CompletedForEmployee plus MaterializeAsync together return exactly one row -- real provider translation, not a mock standing in for it.

concept.title: In-process versus database-side: the same principle, two execution targets
paragraphs: Session 23's GetEmployeeClockEntries filters ClockEntry objects already sitting in .NET memory -- there is no translation step, because the filter IS C# code running directly.

This session's CompletedForEmployee filters rows that may not even be loaded into .NET memory yet -- the filtering happens inside SQLite, and only the matching rows ever cross into .NET as ClockEntryEntity objects.

lab.objective: Add provider-executed EF Core queries and verify them against SQLite.
lab.startingCondition: Session 31 created TimeClockDbContext, entity mapping, and an EF-backed repository with integration-test infrastructure.
steps: In ClockEntryDataQueries.cs, declare a public static class named ClockEntryDataQueries.
Add a public static CompletedForEmployee method that accepts TimeClockDbContext db and int employeeId and returns IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity>.
Start CompletedForEmployee from db.ClockEntries without calling ToList or AsEnumerable.
Add a Where condition matching ClockEntryEntity.EmployeeId to employeeId.
Extend the same provider query with a condition requiring ClockOut to be non-null.
Add startDate and endDate parameters to CompletedForEmployee when the report requires a period boundary.
Extend the provider query with ClockIn comparisons for the requested period.
Return the IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity> without invoking any Domain-only method in the expression.
Add a public static async MaterializeAsync method that accepts IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity> query and an optional CancellationToken.
Inside MaterializeAsync, call ToListAsync(query, cancellationToken) and store the returned List<ClockEntryEntity> in rows.
Return rows in the order required by the caller, making clear whether that ordering occurs in SQL or in memory.
Arrange an open in-memory SQLite database containing multiple employees, periods, and completion states.
Construct the CompletedForEmployee query and assert that no materialized result variable exists before MaterializeAsync is called.
Materialize the query and assert that only the matching employee's completed entries in the period were returned.
Run the focused ClockEntryDataQueriesTests and the full solution test suite.
lab.expectedBehavior: Filtering executes through SQLite with provider-compatible expressions and tested results.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

expectedFiles.why: Keep the lesson synchronized with the cumulative build step.

commit: session-31: teach ef core queries in-memory versus database execution
review: The lab uses mixed because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can CompletedForEmployee's exact same code work against SQLite in tests and (hypothetically) SQL Server in production, with zero changes?
options: IQueryable<T>'s expression tree is provider-agnostic -- each EF Core provider (SQLite, SQL Server, etc.) supplies its own translation from the same expression tree into that database's specific SQL dialect
It cannot -- the code would need to change for each database
SQLite and SQL Server use identical SQL syntax
postQuiz.explanation: This portability is a real, specific benefit of IQueryable's deferred, provider-translated design -- the query-building code stays the same; only the provider registered in PayrollDbContext's options changes.

postQuiz.prompt: If GetEmployeeClockEntries (Session 23's real, in-process IEnumerable<ClockEntry> method) were changed to query a database instead, would its Where clause need to change?
options: Very likely yes -- IEnumerable<T>'s Where runs arbitrary C# in-process, which may not have a SQL equivalent, while IQueryable<T>'s Where must stay within expressions a database provider can translate
No -- IEnumerable and IQueryable queries are always interchangeable
Only the return type would need to change, never the Where clause
postQuiz.explanation: This is exactly why ClockEntry's own GetEmployeeClockEntries staying IEnumerable-based (in-process) versus ClockEntryDataQueries's IQueryable-based (provider-translated) approach are genuinely different techniques, not interchangeable syntax.

postQuiz.prompt: What would happen if MaterializeAsync's OrderBy call ran before ToListAsync instead of after?
options: It would likely still be translated into the SQL query's ORDER BY clause (executing in the database) rather than sorting an already-materialized in-memory list -- a meaningful difference for large result sets
Nothing would change -- OrderBy always executes in .NET regardless of placement
It would cause a compile error
postQuiz.explanation: Chaining OrderBy onto an IQueryable BEFORE materializing lets the database do the sorting; calling it after ToListAsync (as the real MaterializeAsync does) sorts in .NET memory instead -- a real, deliberate implementation choice worth noticing.

reflections: Why does this session's CompletedForEmployee filter on the same three conditions (EmployeeId, ClockOut, date range logic) that the real, in-process GetEmployeeClockEntries also filters on, even though the execution mechanism is completely different?
What would you need to verify before trusting that a LINQ query written against IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity> will translate successfully to SQL, rather than failing at ToListAsync?
Where might mixing IEnumerable-style and IQueryable-style filtering in the same query accidentally force unwanted in-process execution?
whatBreaks: Calling .ToList() (not .ToListAsync()) on an IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity> works but blocks the calling thread during the database round trip instead of yielding it back, losing the benefit of Session 26-28's async/await work. Filtering with a C# method the SQLite provider cannot translate would compile successfully (the expression tree builds fine) but throw only when ToListAsync attempts translation -- a failure that surfaces later than a Session 23-style in-process IEnumerable filter would.
summary: ClockEntryDataQueries.CompletedForEmployee returns IQueryable<ClockEntryEntity> -- an expression tree a database provider translates into real SQL, only executed when MaterializeAsync calls ToListAsync. This is the same deferred-execution principle Session 23 established for GetEmployeeClockEntries's in-process IEnumerable<ClockEntry>, but here the eventual executor is SQLite itself, not the .NET runtime -- confirmed with a real, SQLite-backed integration test, not a mock.
